source_text: Τρυφὴ δὲ εἰς ἡδονὰς ἀλωμένη χαλεπὸν ἀνθρώποις ναυάγιον γίνεται· ἀλλότριον γὰρ τῆς ἀληθοῦς φιλοκαλίας καὶ τῶν ἀστείων ἡδονῶν ὁ ἡδὺς οὗτος καὶ ἀκλεὴς τῶν πολλῶν βίος. φύσει γὰρ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὑψηλόν ἐστι ζῷον καὶ γαῦρον καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ ζητητικόν, ἄτε τοῦ μόνου καλοῦ δημιούργημα, ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ γαστέρα αὐτῷ βίος ἄσεμνός τε καὶ ἐπονείδιστος καὶ εἰδεχθὴς καὶ καταγέλαστος. ἀλλοτριώτατον δὲ τῆς θείας φύσεως ἡ φιληδονία, ὁμοίως μὲν σιτεῖσθαι τοῖς στρουθοῖς, ὁμοίως δὲ τοῖς ὑσὶν καὶ τοῖς τράγοις ὀχεύειν· τὸ γὰρ τὴν ἡδονὴν νομίζειν ἀγαθὸν ἀπειροκαλίας ἐστὶ τελείας, φιλοπλουτία δὲ ἐξίστησι τῆς ὀρθῆς διαίτης τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀπερυθριᾶν πρὸς τὰ αἰσχρὰ ἀναπείθουσα, »ἐὰν μόνον ἔχῃ δύναμιν καθάπερ θηρίον τοῦ φαγεῖν παντοδαπὰ καὶ πιεῖν ὡσαύτως καὶ ἀφροδισίων πᾶσαν πάντως παρέχειν πλησμονήν«. διὰ τοῦτο σπανιαίτατα τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ κληρονομεῖ. ποῦ τοίνυν τὰ τοσαῦτα παρασκευάζονται ὄψα ἢ ἵνα μίαν πλήρωσωσι γαστέρα; τὸ ἀκάθαρτον τῆς γαστριμαργίας οἱ κοπρῶνες ἐλέγχουσιν, εἰς οὓς ἀποπτύουσιν ἡμῶν αἱ γαστέρες τῆς δαιτὸς τὰ λείψανα. ποῦ δὲ τοὺς οἰνοχόους τοὺς τοσούτους συναγείρουσι μιᾷ κύλικι πλησθῆναι δυνάμενοι; ποῦ δὲ τῶν ἐσθήτων τὰς κιβωτούς; τὰ χρυσία δὲ ποῦ; καὶ τὰ κόσμια ποῦ; λωπολδύταις δὲ αὐτὰ καὶ κακούργοις παρασκευάζονται καὶ τοῖς λίχνοις ὀφθαλμοῖς. »ἐλεημοσύναι δὲ καὶ πίστεις μὴ ἐκλειπέτωσάν σε«, φησὶν ἡ γραφή. ἰδοὺ γοῦν καὶ τὸν Θεσβίτην Ἠλίαν καλὸν ὑπόδειγμα τῆς εὐτελείας ἔχομεν, ὅτε »ἐκάθισεν ὑπὸ τὴν ῥάμνον« καὶ ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτῷ κομίζει τροφάς· »ἐγκρυφίας κρίθινος ἦν καὶ καψάκης ὕδατος.« τοιοῦτον ἄριστον αὐτῷ κύριος ἔπεμψεν. ἡμῖν ἄρα ἀνάγκη πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ὁδοιποροῦσιν εὐζώνοις γενέσθαι· »μὴ βαστάζετε γάρ«, εἶπεν ὁ κύριος, »βαλλάντιον, μὴ πήραν μηδὲ ὑπόδημα«, τουτέστι, μὴ πλοῦτον κτήσησθε τὸν ἐν βαλλαντίῳ μονον θησαυριζόμενον, μὴ τὰς ἀποθήκας πληρώσητε τὰς ἰδίας ὡς ἐν πήρᾳ παρατιθέμενοι τὸν σπόρον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς δεομένοις κοινωνήσατε, μὴ ὑποζύγια καὶ οἰκέτας πολυπραγμονεῖτε, οἵτινες ὑποδήματα τῆς πορείας τῶν πλουσίων ἀχθοφοροῦντες ἀλληγορικῶς εἴρηνται. ἀπορριπτέον οὖν τῶν σκευῶν τὸ πλῆθος καὶ τὰ ἀργυρᾶ καὶ τὰ χρυσᾶ ἐκπώματα καὶ τὸν ὄχλον τῶν οἰκετῶν, καλὰς καὶ σεμνὰς παρὰ τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ συνοπαδοὺς αὐτουργίαν καὶ εὐτέλειαν παραλαβόντας· καὶ δὴ βαδιστέον εὐαρμόστως τῷ λόγῳ, κἂν γυνή τῳ παρῇ καὶ τέκνα· οὐκ ἄχθος ἐστὶν ὁ οἶκος συνεπισπέσθαι μαθὼν ὁδοιπόρῳ σώφρονι. σταλτέον δὲ καὶ τὴν φίλανδρον γυναῖκα τἀνδρὶ παραπλησίως, ὁδοιπορικῶς καλὸν ἐφόδιον τῆς εἰς οὐρανοὺς πορείας εὐτέλειαν ἐπιφερομένους μιᾷ σεμνότητι σώφρονι· μέτρον δὲ καθάπερ ὁ ποὺς τοῦ ὑποδήματος, οὕτως καὶ τῆς κτήσεως ἑκάστου τὸ σῶμα· τὸ δὲ περιττόν, ἃ δή φασι κόσμια, καὶ τὰ ἔπιπλα τῶν πλουσίων ἄχθος ἐστίν, οὐ κόσμος τοῦ σώματος. χρὴ δὲ τὸν ἀναβαίνειν βιαζόμενον εἰς τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καλὴν βακτηρίαν τὴν εὐεργεσίαν περιφέρειν καὶ τοῖς θλιβομένοις μεταδεδωκότα τῆς ἀληθοῦς ἀναπαύσεως μεταλαμβάνειν· ὁμολογεῖ γὰρ ἡ γραφή, ὡς ἄρα »λύτρον ἐστὶν ἀνδρὸς ψυχῆς ὁ ἴδιος πλοῦτος«, τουτέστιν, ἐὰν πλουτῇ, μεταδόσει σωθήσεται. καθάπερ γὰρ τῶν φρεάτων ὅσα πέφυκεν βρύειν ἀπαντλούμενα εἰς τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἀναπιδύει μέτρον, οὕτως ἡ μετάδοσις ἀγαθὴ φιλανθρωπίας ὑπάρχουσα πηγή, κοινωνοῦσα τοῖς διψῶσι τοῦ ποτοῦ αὔξεται πάλιν καὶ πίμπλαται, ὃν τρόπον ἐπὶ τοὺς θηλαζομένους ἢ καὶ βδαλλομένους μαστοὺς ἐπιρρεῖν εἴωθε τὸ γάλα. ἀνενδεὴς γὰρ ὁ τὸν παντοκράτορα θεὸν λόγον ἔχων καὶ οὐδενὸς ὧν χρῄζει ἀπορεῖ ποτε· κτῆσις γὰρ ὁ λόγος ἀνενδεὴς καὶ εὐπορίας ἁπάσης αἴτιος. εἰ δέ τις φαίη ἑωρακέναι πολλάκις ἄρτου πενόμενον δίκαιον, σπάνιον μὲν τοῦτο, καὶ ἔνθα οὐκ ἄλλος δίκαιος, ἀναγνώτω δὲ ὅμως κἀκεῖνο· »οὐ γὰρ ἐπ᾿ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ δίκαιος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν τῷ ῥήματι κυρίου«, ὅς ἐστιν ἄρτος ἀληθινός, ἄρτος οὐρανῶν. οὐκ ἄρα ποτὲ ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ ἄπορος, ἕως ἂν ἔχῃ σῴαν τὴν πρὸς θεὸν ὁμολογίαν· πάρεστι μὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ αἰτεῖσθαι καὶ λαμβάνειν ὧν ἂν δέηται παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ἀπολαύειν, εἰ φυλάττοι τὸν υἱόν· πάρεστι᾿ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο, μηδεμιᾶς ἐνδείας αἰσθάνεσθαι. ὁ παιδαγωγικὸς ἡμῶν οὗτος λόγος τὸν πλοῦτον ἡμῖν δίδωσι, καὶ πλουτεῖν οὐ φθόνος τὸ ἀνενδεὲς κτωμένοις δι᾿ αὐτοῦ· ὁ τοῦτον ἔχων τὸν πλοῦτον βασιλείαν κληρονομήσει θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: For luxury, being enslaved to pleasures, becomes a difficult shipwreck for people; for this pleasant and untroubled life of many is foreign to true love of beauty and to noble pleasures. By nature, man is a high and proud animal, seeking what is good, since he is the sole creation of the one who is good; but the life that is centered on the belly is shameful and deserving of blame and disgusting and laughable. Moreover, love of pleasure is most foreign to the divine nature, for it is similar to the way birds are fed and pigs and goats are driven; for considering pleasure to be a good thing is complete lack of beauty, and love of wealth drives a person away from a correct diet, persuading them to rush towards shameful things, saying 'as long as one has the power to eat all sorts of things and drink similarly and to provide every kind of sexual pleasure'. Because of this, a person very rarely inherits the kingdom of God. Where, then, are so many dishes prepared, or to fill one belly? The dung heaps testify to the uncleanness of gluttony, into which our bellies pour the leftovers of our food. Where do they gather so many wine pourers to be filled with one cup? Where are the treasure chests of clothes? Where are the gold and silver ornaments? They are prepared for thieves and evildoers and for the eyes that are evil. 'But let alms and faith not fail you', the scripture says. Behold, we have a good example of frugality in the Thesbite Elijah, when 'he sat under the broom tree' and the angel brought him food; 'it was a cake of barley and a jar of water'. The Lord sent him such a meal. Therefore, it is necessary for us, as travelers on the road to truth, to be well-provided with what is necessary; 'for the Lord said, do not carry a load, or a bag, or sandals', that is, do not acquire wealth that is stored in a load, do not fill your own storehouses like a bag, but share with those in need, and do not be concerned with yokes and slaves, which are allegorically called the sandals of the rich. Therefore, we must reject the multitude of possessions and silver and gold ornaments and the crowd of slaves, and, having received simplicity and frugality from the Pedagogue, we must walk in harmony with the Word, even if a wife and children are present; for a household is not a burden to a traveler who has learned to be self-controlled. And one must also send away a wife who loves her husband, providing a good provision for the journey to heaven, bringing simplicity and self-control in one dignity; and the measure of each possession is like the foot of a sandal, but what is extra, which they call ornaments, and the furnishings of the rich are a burden, not an ornament of the body. But the one who is forced to ascend to heaven must carry a good staff, which is beneficence, and, having shared with those who are afflicted, must receive true rest; for the scripture says that 'wealth is a ransom for a man's soul', that is, if one is wealthy, one will be saved by sharing. Just as the springs that are naturally able to flow, when drawn upon, again fill up the ancient measure, so also the good sharing of philanthropy, being a source, increases and is filled again, sharing with those who thirst for drink, just as the milk flows into the breasts of those who are nursing or have been weaned. For the one who has the all-powerful God's Word is in need of nothing and never lacks anything; for the Word is a possession that is in need of nothing and is the cause of all wealth. But if someone says they have often seen a righteous person in need of bread, this is rare, and where there is no other righteous person, let them nevertheless consider this: 'for the righteous will not live on bread alone, but on the word of the Lord', which is the true bread, the bread of heaven. Therefore, the good person is never in need, as long as they have their confession to God; for they are able to ask and receive what they need from the Father of all, and to enjoy their own possessions, if they keep the Son; and they are also able to not feel any need. Our Pedagogue, the Word, gives us wealth, and to be wealthy is not envied by those who possess what is in need of nothing through Him; the one who has this wealth will inherit the kingdom of God.

choices.why: The Greek word Τρυφὴ refers to a life of luxury and excess.
The Greek word φιληδονία refers to an excessive love of pleasure.
The Greek word εὐτελείας refers to a simple and moderate lifestyle.

pass_b_english: Luxury, enslaved to pleasures, becomes a grievous shipwreck for people; for this sweet and untroubled life of the many is alien to true love of beauty and to noble pleasures. By nature the human being is a lofty and proud creature, a seeker of the good, because he is the sole creation of the Good One; but the life that centers on the belly is shameful, blameworthy, disgusting, and laughable. Moreover, love of pleasure is most alien to the divine nature: it feeds like sparrows and couples like swine and goats; for to consider pleasure a good is perfect lack of beauty, and love of wealth drives a person away from right conduct, persuading him to rush toward shameful things, saying, 'as long as one has the power, like a beast, to eat all kinds of food and drink likewise and to supply every sort of sexual gratification to the full' (cf. Wis 2:6–9). Because of this, one inherits the kingdom of God most rarely. Where, then, are so many dishes prepared, or to fill a single belly? Dung heaps testify to the uncleanness of gluttony, into which our bellies spew the leftovers of our feasting. Where do they gather so many cupbearers, when one cup can be filled? Where are the chests of clothing? Where are the gold and the ornaments? They are prepared for thieves and evildoers and for covetous eyes. 'But let alms and faithfulness not fail you,' says the Scripture (Sir 29:12). Behold, we also have the Thesbite Elijah as a beautiful example of frugality, when 'he sat under the broom tree' and the angel brought him food; 'it was a cake of barley and a cruse of water' (1 Kgs 19:4–6). The Lord sent him such a meal. Therefore it is necessary for us, traveling toward truth, to be well-girt with necessities; 'for the Lord said, Do not carry a purse, no bag, no sandals' (Lk 10:4; Mt 10:9–10) — that is, do not acquire wealth stored in a purse, do not fill your own storehouses as if in a bag, but share with those in need; do not busy yourselves with yokes and slaves, who are allegorically called the sandals of the rich. We must therefore reject the multitude of possessions, silver and gold vessels, and the throng of servants; having received simplicity and frugality from the Pedagogue, we must walk in harmony with the Word, even if a wife and children are present; for a household is no burden to a traveler who has learned to be self-controlled. The husband-loving wife also must be sent forth similarly, bearing simplicity and self-control in one dignity as a good provision for the journey to heaven; and the measure of each one's possession is like the foot to the sandal, but what is superfluous — what they call ornaments — and the furnishings of the rich are a burden, not an adornment of the body. But the one who forces his way up to heaven must carry a good staff, which is beneficence, and, having shared with the afflicted, receive true rest; for the Scripture confesses that 'the ransom of a man's soul is his own wealth' (Prov 13:8), that is, if he is rich, he will be saved by sharing. Just as springs that naturally well up, when drawn upon, again fill the ancient measure, so also the good sharing of philanthropy, being a source, increases and is filled again as it shares with those who thirst for drink, in the way that milk is accustomed to flow into the breasts of those who are nursing or even weaned. For the one who possesses the Word of the Almighty God lacks nothing and never is in need of anything; for the Word is a possession that lacks nothing and is the cause of all wealth. But if someone says he has often seen a righteous man in need of bread, this is rare, and where there is no other righteous man, let him nevertheless consider this: 'for the righteous shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord' (Dt 8:3; Mt 4:4; Lk 4:4), which is the true bread, the bread of heaven. Therefore the good man is never at a loss, as long as he keeps his confession toward God sound; for he is able to ask and receive whatever he needs from the Father of all, and to enjoy his own possessions, if he keeps the Son; and he is also able not to feel any lack. This Pedagogue, our Word, gives us wealth, and to be rich is not envied by those who possess the all-sufficient through Him; the one who has this wealth will inherit the kingdom of God.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Greek text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished version with appropriate scripture citations (Wis 2:6–9, Sir 29:12, 1 Kgs 19:4–6, Lk 10:4, Mt 10:9–10, Prov 13:8, Dt 8:3, Mt 4:4, Lk 4:4) which correspond to the quoted/alluded Greek passages. All nuances regarding the 'Pedagogue', the 'Word', and the metaphors of the 'staff' and 'sandals' are preserved.
